q: What did Philip Zimbardo's 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment set out to explore?
choices: Whether a person's assigned role can change their behaviour
Whether punishment for wrong answers improves memory and learning
Whether prisoners can be rehabilitated through education
Whether students obey professors more readily than police
why: Zimbardo used a coin flip to make 24 screened students 'guards' or 'prisoners' to see if the role itself shapes behaviour. 'Memory and learning' was the cover story of Milgram's study, not Zimbardo's question.

q: What general lesson does Lecture 1 draw from the Eichmann case and the Milgram and Stanford experiments?
choices: Many people will uncritically follow the commands of those in authority
Only people with violent personalities will obey orders to harm others
Ordinary people almost never harm others, even when an authority tells them to
Psychology experiments tell us nothing about real life
why: The slide says it directly: many people uncritically follow those in authority. That is the cost of lacking critical thinking, which the rest of the chapter addresses.
star_note: [14:22-16:22] 'the point is...' many uncritically follow those in power; then asks students to reflect on times superiors ordered them against their beliefs and how they justified it

q: According to Lecture 1, what can happen in everyday life to people who lack critical thinking skills?
choices: Bosses, family or friends may push their own agendas on them
They automatically reach Perry's commitment stage with age
They become immune to pressure from people in power
They start relying too much on reason and evidence
why: He warns that without critical thinking, others can persuade us into careers, universities or even marriages we later regret. Good critical thinking supports a better standard of living.
star_note: [16:22-18:23] spends ~2 min on his own examples: others push agendas so you end up in careers, universities, even marriages you don't want

q: How does the textbook define critical thinking?
choices: A collection of everyday skills needed for full intellectual and personal development
The study of the methods and principles used to distinguish good arguments from poor ones
A belief based on careful personal feelings rather than on outside authority
The single skill of spotting and pointing out other people's mistakes
why: Critical thinking is a collection of everyday skills needed for full intellectual and personal development. The 'methods and principles' wording defines logic, which is only one part of it.
star_note: [18:23] asks students to pause and think what CT is; stresses 'not just one skill, a collection of skills' and repeats it at [24:32-26:33]

q: Critical thinking, according to the lecture, requires learning…
choices: how to think rather than what to think
what to think rather than how to think
which authorities to trust for the answers
to trust your feelings before the facts
why: The slide's phrase is 'how to think rather than what to think': it is about the process of reasoning, not adopting someone else's conclusions.

q: 'The study of the methods and principles used to distinguish correct or good arguments from poor arguments.' Which term is this?
why: That's logic. Critical thinking is the broader collection of skills; logic is one part of it.

q: In Lecture 1, an opinion is defined as…
choices: A belief based only on personal feelings, not reason or facts
A conclusion reached by weighing the reasons and facts on both sides
A belief shared by experts because it is backed by scientific facts
Any statement that can be shown to be either true or false
why: An opinion rests solely on personal feelings rather than reason or fact. That's what separates it from logic and critical thinking.

q: What is the order of Perry's stages of cognitive development, from least to most mature?
why: Students start by deferring to authority (dualism), overcorrect into 'it's all opinion' (relativism), and mature into taking positions on evidence (commitment).

q: 'There are right and wrong answers, and authorities know the right answers.' Which of Perry's stages is this?
why: Dualists see everything as right/wrong or good/bad and look to professors, parents or politicians for the answer. Confirmation bias is a habit of this stage, not a stage itself.

q: Which of Perry's stages holds that when authorities don't have the right answers, everyone has a right to their opinion and there are no right or wrong answers?
why: Relativism rejects the dualist worldview and treats all truth as relative or a matter of opinion. Absolutism is a narrow-mindedness barrier, much closer to dualism.
star_note: [22:30-24:32] restates relativism in his own words ('there is no truth... everything is relative'); calls back to it at [41:00] when explaining his quizzes

q: What marks Perry's commitment stage?
choices: Deciding on the best evidence even though some uncertainty remains
Treating every opinion as equally valid, since there's no objective truth
Looking to professors, parents and politicians for the single right answer
Refusing to take any position until all uncertainty has been removed
why: At commitment you realise not all thinking is equally valid and authorities can be wrong, yet you still commit to positions based on reason and the best available evidence.

q: In a seminar, Jasur says, 'That's just your opinion, and mine is equally true. Who are you to challenge it?' Yet he complains when the professor doesn't back his view. Which stage is this?
why: Relativists treat everything as opinion and look down on challenging others' views. The lecture points out the contradiction: they still expect the professor to support their opinion.

q: After reading studies for and against Tashkent's new paid-parking zones, Malika admits the evidence isn't perfect but concludes they will probably reduce congestion, and says she'd change her mind if new data appeared. Which stage is this?
why: She accepts uncertainty but still takes a reasoned position on the best evidence, while staying open to revision. A relativist would say it's all opinion; a dualist would wait for an authority's answer.

q: Confirmation bias, which the lecture links to the dualistic stage, means…
choices: Seeking only evidence that backs your view, ignoring the rest
Changing your view every time somebody challenges it, to avoid conflict
Asking an authority figure to confirm which answer is the right one
Doubting every claim until it has been proven true
why: Confirmation bias is looking for research, facts and opinions that agree with you while dismissing the rest. Doubting claims until they are shown true is open-minded skepticism, which is a strength.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the eight characteristics of a good critical thinker in Lecture 1?
why: Absolutism is a form of narrow-mindedness, a barrier. The eight are analytical skills, effective communication, research and inquiry, flexibility and tolerance for ambiguity, open-minded skepticism, creative problem solving, being attentive/mindful/curious, and collaborative learning.

q: Open-minded skepticism is also called the 'method of doubt', a term from René Descartes. What does it ask you to do with a claim?
choices: Not take it at face value, but require it to be shown true
Reject it, since most claims turn out to be false
Accept it if most people around you believe it
Ignore it unless it comes from an authority
why: The method of doubt means approaching a claim with an open mind but as a reflective skeptic, asking for it to be proven. It isn't automatic rejection.

q: Which characteristic means giving logical support for your beliefs instead of relying on opinion or experience, and evaluating others' arguments so faulty reasoning doesn't fool you?
why: That's the lecture's description of analytical skills, the first characteristic on the list.

q: The lecture warns that 'too many people defer to others or fail to take a position on a controversial issue simply because they are unable to evaluate conflicting views.' Which characteristic answers this problem?
why: Sorting through conflicting claims takes discernment and tolerance for ambiguity: being patient and able to function when things aren't clear-cut.

q: Viewing problems from multiple perspectives, imagining scenarios in advance, and welcoming risk and even failure as part of reaching a deeper understanding describes…
why: Creative thinkers come up with original solutions, foresee scenarios so they are better prepared, and treat failure as part of the process.

q: In Lecture 1, what does 'collaborative learning' mean as a trait of a critical thinker?
choices: Being open to others' views and seeking solutions good for both sides
Literally studying or doing homework together with classmates in a group
Letting the majority of the group decide so you don't have to think alone
Dividing up the research so that each member covers one part
why: He stresses it's not meant literally. Critical thinking happens in social situations, so you listen to others, anticipate their reactions, lower your own barriers and look for solutions that benefit both sides.
star_note: [30:41] explicitly corrects a misreading: 'we do not just mean... study together... not in the literal terms'; long elaboration on social context

q: What are the three levels of the textbook's three-tier model of thinking, in order?
why: First something happens (experience), then you make sense of it (interpretation), then you raise the level and critically examine that interpretation (analysis).
star_note: [32:50-36:53] asks students to pause and think of barriers, then spends ~4 min on the three tiers with his own job-interview and young-voters examples (other barrier lists he skips)

q: A news report says fewer young people are voting. Your friend immediately says, 'That's because young people just aren't interested in politics.' At which level of the three-tier model is your friend?
why: Your friend is making sense of the experience with a quick, simple reading that may rest on prejudice rather than information. Analysis would ask what's really behind it and what young people actually care about.

q: After his rejection, Timur asks himself: 'Was it really my lack of connections? Or my experience, or how I answered in the interview?' Which level of the three-tier model is this?
why: He is questioning his first interpretation instead of settling for it. Analysis is driven by asking questions.

q: In the textbook, 'resistance' as a barrier to critical thinking is defined as…
choices: The habitual use of immature defense mechanisms when our worldviews are challenged
Rigid beliefs that interfere with critical analysis of our worldviews
Holding two contradictory views at the same time and believing that both are true
Refusing to obey orders from superiors that go against our own moral standards
why: Because most of us dislike being proven wrong, we put up defences to protect cherished worldviews. The 'rigid beliefs' wording defines narrow-mindedness.

q: When does struggling with an issue stop being part of critical thinking and become resistance?
choices: When the struggle becomes an end in itself
When it takes longer than a single day
When you ask other people for their views
When you research the facts before deciding
why: Wrestling with an issue is a normal part of analysis. But when people get lost in details and what-ifs, achieve nothing and lose time, the struggle has become resistance.
star_note: [36:53-38:53] 'Let me just comment on the struggling point' - the only resistance type he explains; adds procrastinators

q: Lecture 1 praised a school director in Nepal who evacuated about 900 pupils minutes before a landslide. What point did this example make?
choices: He acted quickly on the facts instead of struggling
Decisions should wait until every uncertainty is resolved
In a crisis you should obey higher authorities without question
Collaborative learning means consulting everyone before acting
why: He saw the danger was serious and acted at once; ten more minutes might have been fatal. It's the counter-example to struggling as resistance.
star_note: [38:53] his own current-news example (Nepal school director, 900 pupils) to illustrate not struggling

q: Which of these is NOT one of the textbook's types of resistance?
why: Egocentrism is a form of narrow-mindedness. The types of resistance are avoidance, anger, clichés, denial, ignorance, conformity, struggling and distractions.

q: 'Rigid beliefs that interfere with critical analysis of our worldviews' defines which barrier?
why: That's narrow-mindedness, which covers absolutism, fear of challenge, egocentrism, ethnocentrism and anthropocentrism. Resistance is the habitual use of immature defense mechanisms.

q: In Chapter 6, what is an 'issue'?
choices: An ill-defined complex of problems involving controversy or uncertainty
A proposition in an argument that is supported by the other propositions
A statement about why or how something that already happened is the case
A position statement used to win people over
why: An issue is a messy, controversial problem that arguments help us analyse. The other choices describe a conclusion, an explanation and rhetoric.

q: According to the lecture, what goes wrong when an issue is not defined clearly?
choices: The discussion drifts and others can drag you off topic
The argument automatically becomes unsound and has to be dropped
You can then only use descriptive premises, never prescriptive ones
Nothing; clear definition only matters in written essays
why: A vague issue is a slippery path: you drift onto other topics, the other side can steer the discussion wherever it likes, and it can end in frustration. Defining the issue takes clear thinking and good communication skills.
star_note: [12:22] elaborates beyond the slide ('slippery path', opponent can drag you in different directions); repeats in construction step 1 at [38:52] ('the more the issue is clear, the better')

q: You return to your dorm room and your wallet isn't on the dresser. Why does the lecture say 'Who stole my wallet?' is the wrong way to state the issue?
choices: It assumes, without grounds, that someone stole it
It is too neutral and open-ended to lead to any useful answer
It is a conditional statement rather than a genuine question
It focuses on the facts instead of on how you feel
why: All you know is that the wallet is missing; you may have misplaced it or it may be behind the dresser. The neutral issue is 'What happened to my wallet?', and open-mindedness is the trait of good critical thinkers and good detectives.

q: What is the key difference in purpose between rhetoric and argument?
choices: Rhetoric aims to persuade; argument aims to discover the truth
Rhetoric aims to discover the truth; argument aims to persuade
Both aim only to persuade, using different techniques
Rhetoric explains past events; argument predicts future ones
why: Straight from the slide: rhetoric → persuade, argumentation → discover the truth. Rhetoric also starts from a position already taken, while argument starts from an open question.

q: Why should a good arguer resist reducing an issue to two sides, with 'us' as good and 'them' as evil?
choices: Two-sided framing makes effective, creative solutions harder to find
Two sides are too few to keep a debate interesting for an audience
Polarizing an issue makes every premise automatically false
Arguments are only allowed to consider one side of an issue
why: Arguments should stay open to many perspectives. Framing an issue as a fight between two camps, which is common in politics, shuts out the in-between and creative options.
star_note: [18:27] his own politics/religion 'us good, them evil' example; repeats the two-sides warning at [38:52] and [42:55] ('remember to avoid looking at our issue as a contest between two sides')

q: A candidate's campaign video lists only the benefits of his plan, calls his opponents 'enemies of progress', and never mentions any evidence against the plan. This is best described as…
why: It defends a fixed position, polarises the issue into good versus evil, and ignores opposing evidence, all in order to persuade.

q: How do the slides define an argument?
choices: Two or more propositions, one supported by the others
A single proposition that can be shown to be either true or false
A statement about why or how something is the case
An 'if… then…' statement linking two ideas
why: An argument is reasoning made of at least two propositions: the conclusion and the premise(s) that support it. The other choices describe a proposition, an explanation and a conditional statement.

q: What is a proposition?
choices: A statement that expresses a complete thought and can be true or false
A statement that has already been proven true by scientific evidence or observation
A question that opens up an issue for discussion
The main claim that an argument is trying to prove to its audience
why: A proposition only has to be capable of being true or false. 'Toronto is the capital of Canada' is false but is still a proposition. The main claim is the conclusion.
star_note: [20:29] asks students to pause the video and come up with their own propositions

q: Which statement about an argument's conclusion is correct?
choices: It can appear anywhere, at the start as a thesis or at the end
It must always be the final sentence of the argument
It must always be introduced by the word 'therefore'
It is the proposition that gives a reason for another
why: The conclusion is what the argument tries to prove, and it can come first (as a thesis or topic statement) or last. Indicator words help, but they aren't required.
star_note: [20:29] conclusion can come at the start (thesis/topic statement) or end; refers back to it at [42:55] 'thesis statement, like I was mentioning'

q: What is a premise?
choices: A proposition that supports or gives reasons for accepting the conclusion
The proposition that the whole argument is trying to prove to be true
A statement about why or how something we already know happened came about
why: Reasoning runs from the premises to the conclusion. The proposition being proven is the conclusion itself.

q: Descriptive premises are based on…
choices: Empirical facts from observation, science or the five senses
Value statements about what people should or shouldn't do
A comparison between two similar events or things
The definition of a key term that might otherwise be ambiguous
why: Descriptive premises report what is the case, based on observation or science. Value statements are prescriptive, comparisons are analogical, and definitions are definitional.

q: 'It's wrong to cheat on exams' and 'We should strive for diversity on university campuses' are examples of which type of premise?
why: Both are value statements about what's right or what we should do, which makes them prescriptive. They aren't empirical facts.

q: Plato said that just as a charioteer is in charge of his horses, reason should be in charge of our emotions and passions. Which type of premise is this?
why: It works by comparing two similar things (charioteer and horses, reason and passions). The word 'should' is tempting, but what makes it distinctive is the analogy.

q: When does the lecture say a definitional premise is especially important?
choices: When a key term is ambiguous or has several definitions
When the argument relies on scientific observation
When the arguer wants to compare two similar events
When the conclusion is a statement about values
why: If a key term like 'diversity' can mean different things, defining it keeps everyone arguing about the same thing.

q: In a debate about banning phones in class, a student offers the premise: 'Teachers ought to respect students' privacy.' Which type of premise is this?
why: 'Ought to' expresses a value judgement about how people should act, not an observed fact.

q: What is an explanation, and how does it differ from an argument?
choices: It says why or how something is the case; we already know it happened
It tries to prove that something happened by offering premises
It sets a condition with 'if… then…' but draws no conclusion
It defends a position without considering the opposing evidence
why: An argument tries to show that a claim is true. An explanation takes the event as known and tells you its cause or how it came about.

q: Which of these is an argument rather than an explanation?
choices: Bus fares went up and my stipend didn't, so I should cycle.
The bus was late this morning because of an accident on Amir Temur Avenue.
The baby cried because her mother left the room.
The exam was postponed because the professor fell ill.
why: It gives reasons (premises) to support a claim about what you should do. The others take a known event and explain its cause.

q: Why is a conditional statement like 'If you come from Russia, then you speak Russian' not an argument by itself?
choices: No claim or conclusion follows from it on its own
Because every conditional statement is false
Because it contains a premise indicator word
Because it explains why something happened
why: An 'if… then…' statement only links two ideas hypothetically. Nothing is actually asserted as true, so there's no conclusion.

q: In '[I think], therefore [I am]', what is the conclusion?
choices: There is no conclusion, only two premises
There is no premise, only two conclusions
why: 'Therefore' is a conclusion indicator, so what follows it, 'I am', is the conclusion; 'I think' is the premise.

q: Which of these is a conclusion indicator?
why: Conclusion indicators include therefore, thus, hence, so, which shows that, for these reasons, consequently and it follows that. The other three introduce premises.

q: Which of these is a premise indicator?
why: Premise indicators include because, since, for, given that, may be inferred from, the reason is that, as shown by and in view of. Careful: 'for' alone flags a premise, but 'for these reasons' flags a conclusion.

q: 'Students who sit in the front of a class generally earn higher grades. Therefore, you should move up to the front of the class, since I know you want to improve your GPA.' What is the conclusion?
choices: You should move up to the front of the class
Students who sit in the front generally earn higher grades
I know you want to improve your GPA
Students who want higher grades already sit in front
why: 'Therefore' flags the conclusion. The other two stated propositions are premises supporting it.
star_note: [30:41] sets it as an exercise: pause the video and find the propositions, conclusion and premise; make your own examples

q: Which list gives the lecture's five criteria for evaluating an argument?
why: The five criteria are clarity, credibility, relevance, completeness and soundness. Validity and cogency weren't part of this lecture.

q: In a debate on 'Should social media be regulated?', you realise you and your opponent mean very different things by 'regulated'. Which criterion is at stake, and what should you do?
choices: Clarity: ask for clarification of the key term
Credibility: demand scientific evidence for every premise
Completeness: add the missing conclusion yourself
Soundness: declare your opponent's conclusion false
why: If a key term is ambiguous, ask for clarification. As the lecture puts it, 'know the battleground' before you fight on it.
star_note: [30:41-32:41] his own 'battleground' metaphor, repeated: be sure of the battleground, of the definitions of key terms

q: 'When my daughter was young, most doctors were men, so she should give up on becoming a doctor.' What does the lecture say is wrong with this?
choices: The premise is relevant but not sufficient to support the conclusion
The premise is completely irrelevant to medicine
The argument has no conclusion, only an explanation
The premise is a definitional one disguised as a fact
why: A premise can be relevant without giving enough grounds to accept the conclusion, and today many medical students are women.

q: 'Federal funding for education should be allocated by the size of a state. Therefore, Texas should get more federal money than Rhode Island.' What does the lecture use this example to show?
choices: Completeness: the premise 'Texas is bigger' is left unstated
Relevance: the premise is relevant but not sufficient on its own
Clarity: the word 'size' is too ambiguous to evaluate
Soundness: the conclusion has been shown to be false
why: The argument depends on the unstated premise that Texas is larger. Most Americans know that, but for an audience in Uzbekistan you might need to state it.
star_note: [36:49] adds his own local twist: for someone from Uzbekistan you might need to state the 'Texas is larger' premise

q: In the lecture, a sound argument is one in which…
choices: The premises are true and they support the conclusion
The conclusion is true, whatever the premises say
The premises are clearly worded, even if some are false
The arguer succeeds in persuading the audience
why: Soundness needs both: true premises, and a real connection between them and the conclusion based on reason rather than fallacious appeals.

q: What is the first step in constructing an argument?
choices: State the issue clearly, in the form of a question
Establish your conclusion before anything else
Try your argument out on other people
Eliminate any weak or irrelevant premises
why: Clearly stating the issue, worded neutrally as a question, keeps you on track. The conclusion comes only after the premises are settled.

q: 'Prices rose sharply this year; therefore, many families are saving more, since wages have not kept up.' Which word introduces the conclusion?
why: 'Therefore' is a conclusion indicator (like thus, so, hence, consequently), so 'many families are saving more' is the conclusion. 'Since' is the closest trap: it is a premise indicator, introducing a reason ('wages have not kept up'), not the claim being proved.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the lecture's steps for constructing an argument?
choices: Try out your argument on other people
Put your solution into action if needed
why: Looking for indicator words belongs to BREAKING DOWN someone else's argument (identify propositions, conclusion, premises). The construction steps are: state the issue as a question, list premises, eliminate weak/irrelevant ones, establish a conclusion, organize, try it on others, revise, and put it into action if necessary.

q: In the Crime and Punishment passage that opens the lecture, what is Raskolnikov's decision to kill the old pawnbroker based on?
choices: Pure rational calculation of the greatest good, with emotion kept out
A sudden fit of anger after hearing she bit her sister Lizaveta's finger
A revelation he believed came directly from God
Fear that she would report his debts to the police
why: The passage treats it as 'simple arithmetic': one worthless life against thousands helped by her money. The professor's point is that Raskolnikov lets no emotion interfere, and that this is not good critical thinking.
star_note: Lecture 2 [00:03]-[04:11]: opens with the long Dostoevsky passage, asks if it is a good decision for a critical thinker, and comes back to Raskolnikov at [22:38] and [26:44]

q: Which is the lecture's definition of reason?
choices: Supporting a claim or decision on the basis of evidence
The ability to perceive accurately, appraise and express emotion
Belief, trust and obedience directed toward a religious deity
Imagining yourself moving through a structure in space and time
why: Reason is the process of supporting a claim, conclusion or decision with evidence. The other options describe emotional intelligence, faith and spatial-temporal reasoning.

q: Which is the definition of emotional intelligence given in the lecture?
choices: The ability to perceive, appraise, express, understand and regulate emotion
The capacity to enter into and understand the experiences and emotions of other people
The process of supporting a decision on the basis of evidence
The habit of letting feelings make decisions without reasoning
why: Emotional intelligence also includes generating feelings that help thought. Entering into and understanding other people's emotions is empathy, a related but narrower idea.

q: In the lecture, empathy (sympathy) means...
choices: The capacity to enter into and understand others' experiences and emotions
The ability to regulate your own emotions so as to promote intellectual growth
Anger at injustice that pushes you to act
The belief that a problem can be solved
why: Empathy alerts us to oppression and makes us better listeners and communicators. Anger at injustice is moral indignation; believing a problem can be solved is optimism.

q: Fideism is the belief that...
choices: The divine is known through faith, not reason or evidence
Religious beliefs should be consistent with reason and evidence
Faith rests on revelation but must not contradict reason
The existence of God is ultimately unknowable
why: Fideists say faith does not require reason. Accepting revelation while forbidding contradictions with reason is critical rationalism instead.

q: As defined in the lecture, an agnostic is a person who...
choices: Holds that the existence of God is ultimately unknowable
Does not believe in the existence of any personal God at all
Believes faith needs no rational justification
Believes religion must be consistent with evidence
why: An agnostic neither affirms nor denies God, holding the question unknowable. Not believing in a personal God at all is atheism.

q: Most Muslims rejected the 9/11 attackers' 'faith-based' justification on the grounds that such acts are logically inconsistent with God's goodness. Which position does this reasoning illustrate?
why: Their faith rests on revelation, but they use reason to reject a claim that contradicts it. That is critical rationalism: no logical inconsistency between revelation and reason. Plain rationalism would also demand evidence for the faith itself.

q: Lecture 3-2 returns to the Peter Reilly case to illustrate which social error?
why: Police expected that a difficult, belittling mother would drive her son to violence, and reasoned from that expectation to a confession instead of from evidence to a conclusion.
star_note: Lecture 2-1 [00:03]-[04:11]: opens Ch.4 with a long retelling of the Peter Reilly case, then returns to it in Lecture 3-2 [10:15]-[12:22] for social expectations

q: False memory syndrome is...
choices: Vividly recalling events that never happened
Forgetting ordinary days while remembering outstanding events
Believing past outcomes change the odds of a random event
Seeing meaningful patterns in random data
why: We are so suggestible that we can go beyond altering memories to recalling events that never happened. Forgetting ordinary days while recalling outstanding ones is the memorable-events error.

q: Hearsay is...
choices: Evidence heard by one person and repeated to another, and so on
Evidence based on someone's personal testimony of their own experience
Testimony from an expert outside their own field
Evidence that has been reviewed by other experts
why: Hearsay is essentially gossip and is notoriously unreliable. Personal testimony of your own experience is anecdotal evidence instead.

q: A self-styled 'nutrition expert' has 2 million Instagram followers and a busy Telegram channel, but other nutrition scientists don't recognise her work. Which credential is the lecture most emphatic that she lacks?
why: The professor stresses that reputation means recognition by other experts in the field, not YouTube, blogs, Telegram channels or follower counts.
star_note: Lecture 2-1 [16:25]: 'By reputation, I mean...' recognition by peers, not YouTube, blogs, Telegram channels or follower counts (his own local example)

q: Confirmation bias is...
choices: Seeking only evidence that supports what we already believe
Taking personal credit for success and blaming others for failure
Seeing meaningful patterns in random data
Going along with the group's view to fit in
why: It is so strong that we may disregard or reinterpret evidence that contradicts our cherished beliefs. Taking credit for success and blaming others is a self-serving bias.

q: A viral video shows a burnt patch on a piece of non bread that 'looks like' a famous face, and thousands of comments call it a sign. Which error is this?
choices: Misperception that we are in control
why: The brain imposes meaning on a random shape, like the man in the moon or shapes in clouds.

q: Before every exam, Dilshod eats the same breakfast and wears the same blue shirt, convinced this controls how well he does. Which bias is this?
choices: Misperception that we are in control
Exaggerating our strengths and minimising our weaknesses
why: Believing we control events outside our control shows up as superstitious behaviour like lucky shirts and rituals. It is one of the three self-serving biases.

q: Laylo says her A in Calculus came from her intelligence and good study habits, but her D in Physics was because the teacher was unfair and she had the flu on exam day. What is this?
choices: Self-serving bias: credit for success, blame for failure
Confirmation bias: seeking only evidence that supports her view
why: It's nearly the lecture's own example: good grades are put down to herself, poor grades to things outside her control.

q: A lecturer assumes the professional footballer in his class only comes for attendance, so he never calls on him. The student loses interest and gets a mediocre grade, and the lecturer says 'I knew it.' What is this?
choices: Misperception that we are in control
why: The lecturer's own behaviour produced the result he predicted. This is the professor's own example.
star_note: Lecture 3-2 [02:03]-[04:07]: puts himself in the example ('if me, I have this self-fulfilling prophecy') about a footballer student, after the bank-panic example

topic: One of us / one of them
q: The 'one of us / one of them' error is...
choices: Sorting people into 'ours' and 'theirs' and trusting only ours
Following the idea of a high-status group member without checking the evidence
Assuming someone else will help when we are in a crowd
Judging individuals by socially generated group labels
why: We extend respect to people like us and suspicion to those who differ in race, gender, religion, party, age or nationality. Judging individuals by group labels is stereotyping, a related but separate social bias.
star_note: Lecture 3-2 [06:09]-[10:15]: asks students to pause and think of real cases, then about 3 minutes on colonialism, polarisation and an Uzbek-flavoured remedy ('we are all human beings')

q: In a group-project meeting, the student with the highest GPA proposes a framework. Everyone nods along, nobody checks whether it fits the brief, and the project fails. What is this?
why: The group followed its high-status member instead of the evidence. Diffusion of responsibility is about failing to act when a duty isn't assigned, not about converging on an idea.

The ability to use media apps, platforms and tools skilfully and efficiently

q: How does the lecture define a fallacy?
choices: A faulty argument that at first appears to be correct
An argument built on premises that are all false
Any claim that goes against popular opinion
A correct argument that sounds wrong at first
why: A fallacy looks right when you first hear it but turns out to be incorrect on closer examination. The last option is the reverse.

q: What is a formal fallacy?
choices: Reasoning in which the form of the argument itself is invalid
Reasoning that is emotionally persuasive but logically incorrect
An argument that hides weak evidence behind technical language
An argument made in an official setting such as a court
why: Formal means the structure (form) is invalid, whatever the content. 'Emotionally persuasive but logically incorrect' is the definition of an informal fallacy.

q: What is an informal fallacy?
choices: Reasoning that is psychologically or emotionally persuasive but logically incorrect
Reasoning in which the form of the argument itself is invalid, whatever its content
A reasoning mistake made in casual everyday conversation rather than in formal writing
An argument whose conclusion is true even though its premises are false
why: Informal fallacies persuade through psychology or emotion while being logically wrong. An invalid form is a formal fallacy.

q: What lesson does the lecturer draw from the Shannon Townsend case?
choices: Cults hide their aims behind fallacies; stay informed and ask questions
Students with high grades are naturally protected from being manipulated
Religious belief is itself an example of the popular appeal fallacy
Parents should stop their children from moving away for university

q: Into which three families does the lecture sort informal fallacies?
choices: Ambiguity, induction errors, and deduction errors
why: The three families are fallacies of ambiguity, fallacies of relevance, and fallacies involving unwarranted assumptions. Formal fallacies are a separate category, not an informal family.

q: In which family is a premise logically irrelevant to the conclusion, even though it feels psychologically relevant?
why: Fallacies of relevance work because the premise seems related to the conclusion, even though logically it isn't.

q: Which family covers arguments that rest on an assumption not supported by evidence, which weakens the whole argument?
why: An unwarranted assumption is unjustified, so everything built on it is weakened.

q: Which of these is NOT a fallacy of relevance?
why: Slippery slope is a fallacy involving unwarranted assumptions. The other three are all fallacies of relevance in this lecture.

q: What is the fallacy of equivocation?
choices: A key word shifts meaning partway through the argument
Sloppy grammar lets a sentence support two conclusions
The meaning changes depending on which word is stressed
A trait of a whole group is assumed for each member
why: Equivocation: one key term, two meanings, used as if it were one. The other options describe amphiboly, accent and division.

q: 'The sign on the door says No Animals Allowed. We'll find another place for lunch, since humans are also animals.' Which fallacy is this?
why: 'Animals' slides from its everyday sense (pets, non-humans) to its biological sense, which includes humans. This is the lecture's example.

q: 'Two-year-old Katie is very tall. Her father is only average in height. Therefore Katie is taller than her father.' Which fallacy is committed?
why: 'Tall' is a relative term: tall for a two-year-old isn't tall for an adult. Misusing relative terms is equivocation.

q: Which fallacy occurs when a grammatical mistake in an argument allows more than one conclusion to be drawn?
why: Amphiboly is ambiguity in sentence structure, not in one word's meaning (equivocation) or in emphasis (accent).

q: 'Mary's mother and her husband have opposing views.' Which fallacy of ambiguity does this sentence illustrate?
why: The grammar leaves it unclear whose husband is meant, Mary's or her mother's. No single word changes meaning, so it isn't equivocation.

q: A perfume ad says 'Wear it and be happy.' The lecture says the advertiser is exploiting which fallacy?
why: The grammatical 'and' can join two unrelated ideas or imply a cause ('wear it and you'll be happy'). The ad hopes you read in the cause.

q: What is the fallacy of accent?
choices: Meaning changes according to which word or phrase is stressed
A key term takes on a different meaning later in the argument
A sentence's grammar allows two different conclusions
An opponent's position is reworded to make it easier to attack
why: Accent: put the stress on a different word and the claim seems to say something else.

q: 'The university is going to crack down on off-campus drinking. Glad to hear they're OK with on-campus drinking.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The speaker stresses 'off-campus' and infers the opposite about on-campus. Neither the grammar nor any word's meaning changed. This is the lecture's example.

q: What is the fallacy of division?
choices: Assuming a trait of a whole group belongs to each of its members
Generalising about a whole group from a sample that is too small
Splitting a complex issue into only two possible options
Breaking an opponent's argument into pieces and attacking one
why: Division: whole group to individual member. The second option is hasty generalisation and the third is false dilemma.

q: 'Canadians are really nice people. Therefore Derek, who is from Vancouver, must be really nice.' Which fallacy is this?
why: A trait of the group (Canadians) is assumed for one member (Derek). It runs from group to individual, so it is not hasty generalisation. This is the lecture's example.

q: In the lecture, Prof. Muratov said that reasoning 'there are many criminals from Russia, so Russians must be bad people' commits which fallacy?
why: He used national stereotypes like this to illustrate division. Strictly, division runs from the whole group to a member (like the Derek example); reasoning from some members to the whole group is closer to hasty generalisation.

q: What is the key difference between the fallacy of division and hasty generalisation?
choices: Division goes from the whole group to a member; hasty generalisation goes from a few cases to the whole group
Division goes from a few cases to the whole group; hasty generalisation goes from the whole group to a member
Division is a formal fallacy, while hasty generalisation is an informal fallacy
Division concerns emotional appeals, while hasty generalisation concerns word meanings
why: Think of direction: division is group to individual (Canadians to Derek); hasty generalisation is a few individuals to the group (a few abusive men to all men).

q: What is a personal attack (ad hominem) fallacy?
choices: Rejecting an argument by attacking the person who made it
Misrepresenting the opponent's argument to knock it down
Threatening the opponent so that they back down from their view
Changing the subject to avoid answering a hard question
why: Ad hominem tries to create disapproval of the person instead of answering the argument. The others are straw man, appeal to force and red herring.

q: In a TV debate about a tax plan, a candidate says: 'Why would anyone listen to my opponent on taxes? He's been divorced twice and failed at running his own business.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The opponent's private life is attacked instead of his tax plan. His argument isn't restated or distorted, so it's not a straw man.

q: What is an appeal to force (scare tactics)?
choices: Using threats or fear to get someone to accept a conclusion
Evoking sympathy when sympathy is irrelevant to the point
Predicting that one small step will lead to disaster down the line
Attacking the character of the person who is arguing
why: Appeal to force is about threats and fear. Predicting disaster from one small step is slippery slope.

q: A father tells his daughter: 'You don't get to disagree with me while I'm paying your university tuition and putting a roof over your head.' Which fallacy is this?
why: This is the lecture's own example: an implied threat (losing tuition and housing) shuts down disagreement instead of giving a reason why he's right.

q: The lecture uses AI company CEOs, who warn that AI could doom humanity within a decade, as an example of which fallacy?

q: What is an appeal to pity?
choices: Trying to win agreement by evoking sympathy that's irrelevant to the point
Trying to win agreement by threatening the other person with consequences
Trying to win agreement by pointing out that almost everyone already agrees
Trying to win agreement by citing an expert from a completely different field
why: Appeal to pity uses irrelevant sympathy. The others describe appeal to force, popular appeal and inappropriate appeal to authority.

q: Stopped for speeding, a driver tells the police officer: 'Please understand, something terrible just happened at home and I'm not in a good state.' According to the lecture, which fallacy is this?
why: The driver tries to evoke the officer's sympathy, which is irrelevant to whether he was speeding. This is the lecture's example.

q: What is the fallacy of popular appeal?
choices: Treating a conclusion as true because many people believe it or do it
Treating a conclusion as true because an expert in another field says so
Treating a conclusion as true because no one has proven it false
Treating a conclusion as true because a small sample supports it
why: Popularity isn't evidence. The other options describe inappropriate appeal to authority, appeal to ignorance and hasty generalisation.

q: 'God must exist. After all, most people believe in God.' Which fallacy does the lecture say this is?
why: Bandwagon: God's existence doesn't depend on how many people believe. It's not appeal to ignorance, since nothing is said about a lack of proof.

q: What is an appeal to ignorance?
choices: Taking a lack of proof as proof of the opposite
Dismissing an argument because the person making it is uneducated
Ignoring the opponent's argument and changing the subject instead
Relying on what most uninformed people happen to believe
why: It is about absence of proof. Calling the arguer uneducated would be a personal attack.

q: What important exception to the appeal-to-ignorance fallacy does the lecture mention?
choices: In court, a defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty
In science, a theory is accepted until someone disproves it
In religion, beliefs need no proof of any kind
In advertising, claims are true until a regulator rejects them
why: In law, 'not proven guilty' legitimately means treated as innocent, because the burden of proof is on the prosecution.

q: 'UFOs don't exist, as no one has been able to prove that they do.' Which fallacy is this?
why: The lecture's example: no proof that UFOs exist doesn't prove they don't. We simply don't know.

q: What is a hasty generalisation?
choices: Generalising about a group from a sample that is too small or biased
Assuming each member of a group has the traits of the group as a whole
Assuming that because one event came first, it caused the second
Concluding something is true because most people believe it
why: Hasty generalisation is a few cases stretched to the group. The second option is division, the reverse direction.

q: A woman whose father and brothers were abusive concludes that all men are abusers. According to the lecture, which fallacy is this?
why: A few personal cases (a small, biased sample) are stretched to cover all men. Division would go the other way, from a group trait to one member.

q: What is a straw man fallacy?
choices: Attacking a distorted version of the opponent's argument
Changing the subject to a different issue to escape the original argument
Attacking the opponent's character instead of the argument they made
Using one weak example to make a generalisation about everyone
why: The straw man is the distorted version of the argument. The other options describe red herring, ad hominem and hasty generalisation.

q: 'Mamdani wants free public transport and to tax the rich. He supports socialism. But socialism was already tried and failed in the Soviet Union. Therefore his argument is invalid.' Which fallacy is this?

q: What is the difference between a straw man and a red herring?
choices: A straw man attacks a distorted version of the argument; a red herring changes the subject to another issue
A straw man changes the subject to another issue; a red herring attacks a distorted version of the argument
A straw man attacks the person's character; a red herring attacks the person's family or friends
A straw man is a fallacy of relevance; a red herring is a fallacy of ambiguity
why: Both are fallacies of relevance. The straw man stays on topic but distorts it; the red herring leaves the topic.

q: Which fallacy tries to sidetrack an argument by going off on a tangent and raising a different issue?
why: Sidetracking to a different issue is a red herring. A straw man stays on the issue but distorts it.

q: 'Why are you upset about my driving after a few drinks? It's not a big deal. Look at all the accidents caused by people talking on their phones.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Instead of defending drink-driving, the speaker drags attention to phone use, a different issue. Nobody's argument is distorted, so it's not a straw man. This is the lecture's example.

q: What is begging the question?
choices: Assuming the conclusion is true by making it the same as a premise
Asking a question that presumes the answer to an unasked question
Asking so many questions that the opponent eventually gives up
Reducing a complex issue to just two possible choices for the listener
why: Despite the name, it has nothing to do with asking questions. A question that presumes an answer is a loaded question.

q: Begging the question is also known as...
why: The argument goes in a circle: the conclusion is used to support itself. Post hoc is questionable cause; either/or is false dilemma.

q: 'Capital punishment is wrong because it is immoral to inflict death as a punishment for a crime.' Which fallacy is this?
why: 'Immoral to inflict death as punishment' just restates 'capital punishment is wrong'. It defines the key term rather than giving a reason. This is the lecture's example.

q: What is an inappropriate appeal to authority?
choices: Relying on an expert from the wrong field
Rejecting an expert's view because of the expert's personal life or past
Assuming something is true because the majority believes it
Using a powerful person's threat to force someone to agree
why: The fault is borrowing authority from the wrong field. Rejecting an expert over their private life would be ad hominem.

q: A popular lifestyle blogger is invited onto a podcast as 'today's expert' and explains how the national economy should be managed. Listeners treat her advice as authoritative. Which fallacy is this?

q: What is a loaded question?
choices: A question that already assumes the answer to a question nobody asked
An argument whose conclusion just repeats one of its premises
A question that offers only two answers to a complex issue
A question asked to move the discussion away from the real issue at hand
why: The hidden, unasked question is the trap. Offering only two options is false dilemma.

q: In court, a lawyer demands: 'Have you stopped beating your wife? Answer yes or no.' Which fallacy is this?
why: Either answer admits he has beaten her. The question presumes the answer to the unasked question 'Did you ever beat her?'. This is the lecture's example.

q: What is a false dilemma?
choices: Presenting only two options when more exist
Predicting that one step will lead to extremes
Assuming the answer to an unasked question
Distorting the opponent's view to defeat it
why: A false dilemma hides the other options. The rest describe slippery slope, loaded question and straw man.

q: 'Why do you complain about our politics? If you don't like our policies, you can leave the country.' Which fallacy is this?
why: It offers only two choices, accept everything or leave, and ignores voting, debate or reform. This is the lecture's example.

q: What is the fallacy of questionable cause?
choices: Assuming without evidence that one thing caused another
Assuming that allowing one action will lead to all its extreme forms
Assuming that something natural must be good or acceptable
Assuming that a group's traits belong to each of its members
why: Questionable cause is about unsupported causal links. The others are slippery slope, naturalistic fallacy and division.

q: 'I wore my lucky jacket to the exam and got an A, so I'll wear it to every exam from now on.' According to the lecture, this superstition is an example of which fallacy?

Questionable cause says allowing one step leads to the extremes; slippery slope asserts an unproven causal link
Questionable cause is a fallacy of relevance; slippery slope is a fallacy of ambiguity
Questionable cause concerns only past events; slippery slope concerns only natural events

q: What is a slippery slope fallacy?

Claiming that one event caused another because it happened first
Claiming that only two options are available on a complex, many-sided issue
Claiming that one bad case proves that a whole group is bad

why: His examples are Nike shoes and iPhones among young people; the textbook even reports US cases of theft and murder over such items. Snob appeal is narrower: linking the product to attractive or successful people.

q: A payment app's billboard in Tashkent: 'Join the 5 million Uzbeks who already pay with us!' Which fallacy is this?
why: The message is 'everyone is doing it, so you should too'. Being popular doesn't make an app good or safe.

q: Snob appeal in advertising means:
choices: Linking the product with attractive, strong or successful people and a desirable lifestyle
Claiming that nearly everyone around you, your classmates and neighbours, already owns the product
Having a famous person give expert advice on something outside their own field
Exaggerating the product with words like 'miracle' and 'must-see'
why: Snob appeal sells an image: buy this and you join the beautiful, strong, successful people. 'Everyone has it' is ordinary popular appeal.

q: A beer commercial shows only good-looking, laughing young people at a rooftop party overlooking Tashkent City. Which fallacy is it mainly using?
why: It ties the drink to an attractive, fun lifestyle. That's his own example: alcohol ads showing drinkers as happier and having more fun. It doesn't claim everyone drinks it, so it isn't plain popular appeal.

q: A famous Uzbek pop singer stars in a bank ad, explaining that this bank's deposit rates are 'the smartest financial decision you can make'. Which fallacy is this?
why: She is presented as giving financial advice, which is outside her expertise. If the ad only showed her glamorous life with the bank card and gave no advice, snob appeal would fit better.

q: A washing-powder ad shows only women doing laundry and ends with: 'Every good wife knows the secret of white shirts.' Which fallacy is this?
why: It reinforces a stereotype about what women do and what makes a 'good wife', which the lecture files under hasty generalization.

q: What is amphiboly, as the lecture applies it to ads?
choices: Ambiguous grammar that allows more than one reading
Swapping harsh words for softer, less offensive ones
Exaggerating a product with words like 'miracle'
Using numbers that are true but misleading out of context
why: Amphiboly is about sentence structure, not word choice. Swapping words for softer ones is euphemism.

q: An online shop advertises: 'Free delivery in Tashkent and the regions on orders over 200,000 sum.' A Tashkent customer orders for 80,000 sum and is charged for delivery; the shop says the minimum applies everywhere. What's the problem with the ad?
choices: Amphiboly: the sentence can be read two ways
Euphemism: 'free' is a softer word for a fee
why: It can mean 'free in Tashkent, and free in the regions over 200,000' or 'free everywhere over 200,000'. That grammatical ambiguity, which the shop then reads in its own favour, is amphiboly.

q: A cigarette brand advertises '100% natural tobacco, no additives'. Which fallacy does the lecturer say this commits?
why: This is his own example. Even natural tobacco harms your health, so 'natural' says nothing about safety. The persuasion rests on the word 'natural', not on exaggeration.

q: Replacing words for an unpleasant reality with softer, less scary or less offensive ones, while still leading to the same conclusion, is:
why: Euphemism is substitution of words. It's the opposite move from hyperbole, which inflates rather than softens.

q: A microloan company's ad calls its high-interest loans 'a friendly financial helping hand'. Which technique is this?
why: A costly debt gets a soft, friendly label. The product is the same; only the words are less scary.

q: A plov centre's sign: 'The best plov in the universe. A must-try!' Which fallacy is this?
why: Pure exaggeration, the same pattern as his 'must-see cinema' and 'must-go place'.

q: A car ad says: 'Our cars are like stone.' Why does the lecturer call this a weak analogy?
choices: Stone lasts for centuries, but a car loses value within 5–10 years
Stone is natural, and natural things aren't always good
The slogan's grammar can be read in two different ways
'Stone' is a softer word that hides how heavy the car is
why: The cars share almost nothing with stone that matters to a buyer, so the comparison falls apart. The other choices describe the naturalistic fallacy, amphiboly and euphemism.

q: A study centre advertises: '98% of our students passed the IELTS!' You later learn only 40 students sat the exam, after weaker students were told not to take it. Which issue is this?
choices: Hasty generalization from a small sample
why: The 98% may be technically true, but it hides who was counted. True-but-misleading numbers are the lecture's 'logic & statistics' problem; hasty generalization in ads, per the lecture, is about stereotypes.

q: According to the lecture, science is the use of reason to move from:
choices: Observable facts to hypotheses to testable explanations
Accepted paradigms to laws that can never again be questioned
Personal experience and intuition to moral values
Expert opinion to popular agreement on what is true
why: That's the slide definition. The facts are the data; the end product is an explanation that can be tested.

q: The belief that our physical senses are the primary source of knowledge, so that more data and observations mean better explanations of nature, is:
why: Empiricism treats the empirical method, knowledge gathered from the physical world through the senses, as the only reliable way to know.

q: The assumption that we can study the physical world as an object outside us, without bias, so that systematic observation will lead scientists to agree, is:
why: Objectivity assumes the scientist stands outside what they study, which supposedly puts them in a neutral position. Kuhn later challenges this.

q: The assumption that everything in the universe is made of physical matter is:
why: Materialism is the working assumption of most scientists. Dualism adds a separate non-material, spiritual realm.

q: The assumption that the universe is orderly, made of interconnected causal relationships we can discover through systematic observation and inductive reasoning, is:
why: Predictability is about orderly cause and effect. Unity, which is linked to it, is the further belief in one underlying structure in everything.

q: The assumption that there is an underlying unified, dynamic structure present in all things is:
why: Unity goes beyond predictable causes: it says one structure runs through all phenomena.

q: Which philosopher argued that we only have an idea in our mind of a world outside us, not direct evidence that this world actually exists?
why: The lecture uses Descartes as the first limitation of science. Kuhn wrote about paradigms, Wegener proposed continental drift, and Copernicus heliocentrism.
star_note: [08:08] asks students to pause the video and think of objections to the assumptions before giving the limitations

q: Which position on science and religion does the lecture say most scientists and Western philosophers hold?
choices: Science always trumps religion when they conflict
Religion always trumps science when they conflict
They work in separate, mutually exclusive realms
They concern the same reality and complement each other
why: Position one. It created antagonism with fundamentalist religion, which reads scripture as the literal word of God, and helped produce the opposite camp (religion trumps science).
star_note: [12:10]-[20:27] calls science vs religion 'more interesting ... controversial', spends ~8 min on the four positions and adds a podcast link

q: 'Science asks how and what; religion asks why.' Which position on science and religion is this?
why: In the third position, science deals with objective, empirical reality and religion with values and subjective, spiritual reality, so they don't overlap.

q: A theologian says: 'If a verse seems to conflict with well-established science, we should reinterpret the verse, because faith and science describe one reality from different sides.' Which position is this?
choices: Science always trumps religion in a conflict
Religion always trumps science in a conflict
why: Reinterpreting scripture when it clashes with science is the fourth position. It isn't 'science trumps religion', because the aim is for both to converge and inform each other, not to discard religion.

q: What is the correct order of the scientific method's steps?
choices: Problem → hypothesis → gather info and refine → test → evaluate
Hypothesis → problem → gather info and refine → test → evaluate
Problem → test → hypothesis → evaluate → gather info and refine
Gather info and refine → problem → hypothesis → evaluate → test
why: You need a problem before an explanation, you refine the explanation before testing it, and you evaluate only once you have results.

q: A master's student searches Google Scholar and journal databases to see what's already known about youth unemployment in Uzbekistan and where the gaps are. Which step of the scientific method is she on?
choices: Gathering information to refine the hypothesis
why: He puts the literature review in step one: it shows whether someone already solved the problem and where the gaps are. Refining comes later, once you already have a hypothesis.
star_note: [22:37] long personal advice on step 1: master's/PhD, literature review, Google Scholar, finding gaps

q: A proposed explanation for a particular set of phenomena is a:
why: A hypothesis is the initial proposed explanation (step two). It becomes part of a theory only after it has been tested and supported many times.

q: An explanation of some aspect of the natural world, based on well-substantiated facts, laws and tested hypotheses, is a:
why: A theory rests on hypotheses that have already been tested. His examples are relativity and human capital theory.
star_note: [24:40] illustrates 'theory' with human capital theory 'from my own subject' (reused at [34:52])

q: Which five criteria does the lecture use to evaluate a hypothesis?
choices: Popular, natural, well-funded, quickly published, peer-approved
why: In full: relevant to the problem, consistent with well-established theories, simplest, testable and falsifiable, and predictive. The second list is the assumptions of science, and the third is the steps of the scientific method.
star_note: [26:43] says hypotheses 'play a crucial role' and we should know how to evaluate them, then goes through each criterion

q: A student researching why IUT students skip morning classes ends up adding hypotheses about global oil prices and national GDP, because she never clearly defined her problem. Which criterion is she failing?
why: A hypothesis must relate to the phenomenon it explains. He warns that a vague, too-broad problem leads down a 'slippery path' of off-topic hypotheses and conclusions.

q: If two rival hypotheses both meet the basic criteria, which one do scientists generally accept?
why: The lecture calls this a logical principle well known among scientists (usually called Occam's razor).

q: A researcher checks whether human capital theory, developed in the USA in the 1960s, also predicts that better-educated workers in Uzbekistan earn more. What does this show about a good theory?
choices: It can predict the outcome of similar events in a new context
Once accepted, it no longer needs to be checked against data
It only applies in the country where it was first developed
Applying it in another country turns it into pseudoscience
why: His own example of predictive power: a well-established theory lets you predict results elsewhere, and then test whether they hold.
star_note: [34:52] repeats his human capital example, applied to the Uzbek context, for predictive power

q: Why is falsifiability, rather than confirmation, used as the test of a good scientific explanation?
choices: Nothing can be proven 100% true, but a claim can be shown false
Confirming a hypothesis is considered unethical in modern research
Falsified hypotheses are simpler and therefore always preferred
Only hypotheses that have been falsified can become new paradigms
why: No number of confirming cases gives certainty, but one counter-example can refute a claim. A good hypothesis must also be testable and replicable by other scientists.

q: The hypothesis 'all swans are white' was based on observing thousands of white swans. What happened, and what does it show?
choices: One black swan proved it false, showing the claim was falsifiable
Thousands more white swans confirmed it with 100% certainty
It was rejected for not being the simplest explanation
It became a paradigm because it had many followers
why: It took only one non-white swan to refute it, and black swans were later found. That's the lecture's example of why falsifiability, not confirmation, is the test.

q: A body of explanations that masquerades as science to gain legitimacy, but rests on emotional appeals, superstition and rhetoric, is:
why: Science grounds its explanations in systematic observation, reason and testing. Pseudoscience only borrows its look.

q: A researcher first surveys 500 students, then invites 20 of them for in-depth, face-to-face interviews to understand their answers better. Which research design is this?
why: This is the lecture's example of mixed methods: surveys give quick, basic answers, so interviews add depth for a more balanced result.

q: Research participants agreeing of their own free will to take part, knowing the full consequences of the study, is called:
why: Informed consent is the first data-collection issue on the slide.

q: A study claiming 'we are very close to AGI' turns out to be funded by an AI company. What should a critical thinker ask first, according to the lecture?
choices: Who funded the study, and who benefits from its claims?
Was the study published quickly enough?
Did the participants give informed consent before the study?
Is the hypothesis the simplest one available?
why: This is the neutrality of science. Political pressure and private or business funding can bias research, so always check who is behind a study.
star_note: [47:09] his recurring AI-company example ('we are close to AGI'): check who funded the research

q: 'Publish or perish' refers to:
choices: Pressure to publish a quota of papers to keep your job or get promoted
A rule that findings must be published within a year or else destroyed
The way old paradigms die out once new research is published
Pseudoscientists losing their followers once real studies appear
why: It comes from KPIs and metrics at universities: publish enough to keep the job, get promoted or earn more. The lecture names it as one driver of today's ethical problems in science.
star_note: [43:05]-[47:09] spends ~4 min on publish or perish: IUT 10-papers KPI, Einstein's 5-6 papers a year, AI use

q: Kuhn challenged the idea that:
choices: The scientific method is objective and science is steadily progressive
Science is a social construct shaped by the society that produces it
Paradigms shape what scientists see and which problems they study
Progress in science comes through crises and paradigm shifts
why: The other three are things Kuhn argued for. What he attacked was the picture of science as purely objective and moving steadily forward.

q: Research firmly based on past scientific achievements, which a scientific community accepts for a time as the foundation for its further work, is:
why: Normal science is what fills journals and textbooks. Its achievements supply the paradigms researchers work within.

q: For Kuhn, the accepted view of what the world is like and how we should go about studying it is a:
why: A paradigm is the shared worldview and model for research. Normal science is the research done within it.

q: A paradigm shift in which a new scientific theory replaces a problematic paradigm is called:
why: This is Kuhn's third concept. Revolutions break up long periods of normal science.

q: Copernicus's theory that the Earth goes around the Sun replaced the Earth-centred view of the universe. In Kuhn's terms, this was:
choices: Normal science building on the past
why: A new theory replaced a problematic old paradigm. The lecture uses Copernicus as the revolution of his time.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the limitations of science given in the lecture?
choices: Scientific instruments always distort what they measure
Empiricism limits science to what can be observed
Observation alone can't prove a necessary causal link
Quantum mechanics questions that the universe is orderly
why: The slide's limitations are: Descartes (we only have an idea of the outside world), empiricism limits science to the observable, observation can't establish a necessary causal connection, our experience of reality depends on our brains, and quantum mechanics. He mentions instruments only as extensions of our senses that still miss things like dark matter; he never says they distort, so that is the odd one out.
star_note: [08:08] asks students to pause the video and think of objections to the assumptions before giving the limitations

q: A student's hypothesis contradicts several well-established theories in her field, and she cites none of them. Her supervisor warns she will get little validation from the research community. Which criterion for a good hypothesis is she failing?
choices: Relevance to the problem under study
why: A good hypothesis is consistent with well-established theories, and he advises new researchers to build on them to get validation from the research community. Relevance is the closest distractor, but her hypothesis can be on-topic and still clash with established theory.
